new_statements.quote: Grassfields Bantu languages have some of the most complex tone systems of any group of languages in Africa. [...] All GB languages have at least four levels: high (H), mid (M), low (Ln), and low that falls (L). The mid tone in most languages is a downstepped high (↓H), with each new ↓H establishing a new ceiling for all following H tones. So most GB languages contrast a HH sequence from a H↓H sequence. [...] Most languages also have two different L tones, one that falls before pause, and the other that remains level. [...] However, within Mbam-Nkam, for various languages in the Ngemba group, and for Bafanji in the Nun group the level low tone is not present. Instead of having a floating [L] following an L, the LH sequence is realized as a rising tone on the surface (Elias et al. 1984:62-70).
new_statements.citation: Watters, John R. 2003. Grassfields Bantu. In Derek Nurse & Gerard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages (Routledge Language Family Series), ch. 14, 225-256. London: Routledge. [read from the publisher's companion-website PDF '' (chapters 14-31, 491 pp.) for the 2nd-edition ISBN 9781138799677]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. Watters 2003 sec. 2.4 speaks of 'All GB languages' / 'most GB languages'; Beba' appears only in the chapter's language list (as a Bafut/Ngemba lect), so this is a Grassfields-wide characterisation, not a Beba'-specific statement (the searcher's own rule_in_words says FAMILY-LEVEL ONLY). | checker: URL re-checked through the compiler gate (HEAD): HTTP 200, Content-Type application/pdf, Content-Length 4,884,157 = size of the saved mirror file; no login, publisher companion-site copy ('Copyright Material - Provided by Taylor & Francis' on every page) -> access open, contents comparative-historical (family survey chapter) both acceptable. Quote located in…
new_statements.relation_note: Tone: family-wide >=4 surface levels, downstep, floating tones, two L tones (level vs falling) except in various Ngemba languages; Bafut H, M, L, Ln. Stress/accent: nothing. Syllable structure CV, CVC, CSV, CSVC, V/N syllabic prefixes (sec. 2.1).
new_statements.rule_in_words: FAMILY-LEVEL ONLY: every Grassfields Bantu language (a set that, by the chapter's own list, includes Beba' as a Bafut dialect within Ngemba) is a tone language with at least four surface pitch levels (H, M = mostly downstepped H, level L, falling L) deriving from a historical H/L system with floating tones; in several Ngemba languages the level-L vs falling-L contrast is absent and L+floating H surfaces as a rise; sister language Bafut has H, M, L, Ln (Mfonyam 1982). Nothing is said about word stress or accent anywhere in the chapter (the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur in ch. 14).
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed (no stress discussion at all)
new_statements.exceptions: Aghem deletes certain L tones (Hyman 1987); Center/East Ring and southern Bamileke have a true M instead of downstepped H; Meta' has a 'raised low'; Ngemba-group languages and Bafanji lack the level L (Elias et al. 1984).
new_statements.identity_note: Family-level overview of all Grassfields Bantu. Beba' [bfp] is explicitly inside its scope but appears only in the sec. 1 classification list (p.232): under (b) Ngemba, '(ii) Bafut (d:Bufe Afughe, Bafut)(d:Beba' (a:Mubadji(n:Baba'zhi))) 50,000 (1987) (Batadji, Shishong, Babadji, Bebadji, Bazhi, Biba)', i.e. treated as a dialect of Bafut. The chapter contains no Beba' data; its tone statements are universal claims over 'all GB languages' plus a remark on 'various languages in the Ngemba group' (sourced to Elias et al. 1984) and on Bafut (Mfonyam 1982). Not in Glottolog's beba1238 list (it is a Glottolog reference for Grassfields generally).

sources.note: No phonology of Beba'. In a survey of early reports of tone and drum languages it quotes District Officer Cantle (1932): 'Like the remainder of the clans of Widekum, the Age, Befang, and Beba peoples are acquainted with the drum language. The Age clan and the villages of Batomo, Mubadji and Bakaw can also send messages by voice, pitched as a kind of yodel, and by whistle. The Befang clan and the village of Mukuru have lost this art.' Second-hand ethnographic evidence of tone-based speech-surrogate signalling, not a statement about the number of tones or about word stress.
